full_judgment:
3. Plaintiff filed suit on 24th November for a claim of Taka 24 lacs and odds. As has been noticed he filed an application for attachment before judgment. Pubali Bank challenged the attachment order and prayed for vacating it. This was refused by the trial Court in Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 1 of i984. On 29th March 1984 the suit was decreed ex-parte and the plaintiff decree-holder filed Money Execution Case No. 56of 1984. 

 4. Since the trial Court dismissed the Miscellaneous Judicial Case No.1 of 1984 the Pubali Bank moved the High Court Division, Chittagong Session in Civil Revision No. 152 of 1987. The High Court Division came to the conclusion that the attachment order was bad and vacated it and further struck off the Execution Case No. 56 of 1984- as well. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider three submissions : (1) whether the Bank could secure release of attached goods even though it: was a pledgee, (2) . whether the plaintiff could retain scrap as bailee under section 170 of the Contract Act till he receive his remuneration and (3) whether the High Court Division was justified in giving a direction for striking off the Money Execution Case No. 56 of 1984. 

 9. Now Mohammad Meah, the breaker, became alert to the situation when his dues remained unpaid.He filed the money suit on 24th November, 1983 for Taka twenty four lacs and odds and the scraps in the ship yard was only valued at Taka eight lakhs and odds. He filed an application under Order 38 Rule 5 for attachment before judgment. It is necessary to detail here as to the scope of such petition under Rule 5. This is a prayer for attachment before judgment. Such prayer is allowed very sparingly be- cause the jurisdiction is rather extra-ordinary and it is exercised with utmost care. In this case the trial Court granted the prayer despite the objection of the Bank. Be it noted that the Bank filed an application under Order 38, Rule 8 for investigation of claim to property attached before judgment and it was numbered as Misc. Judicial Case No.1 of 1984. The High Court Division not only vacated the attachment order but struck off the execution case as well. It is re-assuring to see in the judgment of my learned brother a direction that the money execution case will follow its own course that means decree remains intact. As a matter of fact this decree was passed ex-parte. 

 12. The learned Counsel appearing for the Bank has frankly stated that the cash credit account has been liquidated considerably and only 16 Lakh is owed to the Bank. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submitted that remuneration of the ship breaker Mohammad Mcah is still due and the claim is 24 lakhs for which the decree has been passed. In the majority decision of this Court, this decree remains intact. The crux of the problem as to how he could execute the decree when all the properties of the Janapad Enterprise is mortgaged to the Bank. The only available property was the scheduled property which was valued for only eight lakh. The question was whether the plaintiff could retain this property. Plaintiffs claim for his remuneration is grounded on lien and section 170 says that he has a right to retain such goods until he receives due remuneration for the services in the absence of the contract to the contrary. Is there any contract to the contrary in this case between the Bank and the borrower that the remuneration of the breaker must not be given out of the sale proceeds of the ships? The answer is in the negative. If so then why the ship breaker will be deprived of his remuneration. It was contended by the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent that in the application for attachment the plaintiff did not mention the word 'lien' nor did he do so in his written objection to the application filed by the Bank for vacating that order. To say the least rule of pleading docs not warrant it. In England under RSC Order 18 Rule 11 "a party may by his pleading raise any point of law. There is a vital distinction between pleading law, which is not permitted and raising a point of law in a pleading which is permitted under RSC Or. 18, r. 11. Pleading law obscures or conceals the facts of the case; raising a point of law defines or isolates an issue or question of law on the facts as pleaded (Annual Practice, 1965 P 370)." A party may at the trial raise a point of law open to him even though not pleaded (See Independent & Co. Vs. Knowles 1962 3, All ER 27). Hence the objection that has been taken that the plaintiff did not mention lien in his pleading to my mind becomes untenable. 

 13. The upshot of the while discussion is that Bank's right has not been affected by such attachment order. Since the suit has been decreed the lien of the plaintiff for retaining the goods for his remuneration remains unchallenged because there is no contract to the contrary between the Bank and the borrower. To say that the remuneration for breaking cannot be paid unless Bank's total debt is liquidated sounds untenable. To hold to the contrary is to bring the proposition in absurdity, inasmuch as, the bank granted the loan for buying the ship and the ship is to be scrapped and the scrap is to be sold in the market and the sale proceeds is to be deposited into cash credit account for liquidating the debt. Unless the ship is broken how the debt is to be liquidated? Therefore, the question comes what about the remuneration of the ship breaker and the law says in section 170 of the Contract Act that he can retain such goods. The argument of the Bank that the plaintiff knew about defendant's transaction with the Bank that the vessel with its materials are pledged to the Bank. This argument is wrapped up in syllogism because did the Bank know as to who was breaking the ship, the answer obviously is in the affirmative. The Bank knew that Mohammad Meah was breaking the ship hence it is Bank's right Vs. Mohammad Meah lien and section 170 says in the absence to the contrary Mohammad Meah's lien gets the priority because such lien is particular lien. Moreover these scheduled articles are in actual possession of the' plaintiff as scrap. Lien cannot be a ground for action, it can be taken as defence. Precisely that was done here in Misc. Judicial Case No. 1 which was brought to the Bank. Here the plaintiff can raise the point of lien in the face of the application for releasing the attached properties. And that has happened in this case. 

 15. Secondly the labour or skill must have been exercised in accordance with the purpose of bailment. Now what was the purpose in this case.Obviously to break the ship and reduce into scraps. 

 18. This case is on all forces with the present case. Pubali Bank, allowed the Janapad Enterprise to reduce the ship into scrap and the plaintiff was engaged to do it. Here the Janapad was the bailor and Mohammad Meah the bailee and the purpose of bailment was to break the ship into scrap. What plaintiff did was within the scope of bailment. There is no evidence that in the contract between Janapad and the Pubali Bank, such lien was excluded. 

 22. The Court noticed the earlier decision in Green Vs. All Motors Ltd. (1917, 1 K.B. 625) where it was held that the defendants had a lien on the car as against the plaintiff for the cost of the re- pairs It in turn approved the earlier decision in Koone Vs. Thomas (1905) 1 K.B. 136. But in Albemarle's case (1928, 1 K.B. 307) the plaintiff contended that the decisions in the earlier cases have no application because in their contract there was a special clause against creating lien. Sargant L. J. observed: "They wanted to establish that their special clause got over the decision in Cree v. All Motors Ltd., (1917,1 K.B. 625)," But it was repelled. 

 23. Applying these principles I have no hesitation in allowing the appeal inasmuch as the appellant Mohammad Meah had pleaded lien in Miscellaneous Judicial Case for his remuneration rightly and he was not aware of any special clause against creating lien in the contract between the Pubali Bank and Janapad Enterprise. 

 24. To sum up : (i) Plaintiffs petition under Order 38 Rule 5 was misconceived. 

 (ii) Pubali Bank's petition under Order 38, Rule 8 gave rise to Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 1 of 1984. In that case the plaintiff could, and as a matter of fact did take the plea of lien as defence. 

 25. As has been noticed that in the judgment of my learned brother M.H. Rahman, J, the order of striking down the money execution case has been set aside and in that view of the matter the question whether the attachment before judgment was necessary loses its importance. When in an appeal two questions arc debated, namely, whether the attachment order was bad and the money execution case was validly filed, Superior Court in dealing with the appeal though takes the view that the interlocutory matter as unjustified e.g. attachment order and allows the execution case to proceed its normal course, the appeal is allowed in usual course. Hence the appeal should have been allowed with the lien that has been given by law under section 170. 

 27. M.H. Rahman, J.- This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 5th July, 1987 of the High Court Division, Chittagong Sessions, passed in Civil Revision No. 152 of 1987 reversing the judgment and order dated 26th February, 1986 of the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 108 of 1984 that arose out of Money Suit No. 137 of 1983. 

 28. The appellant instituted the suit on 24th November, 1983 in the Court of Subordinate Judge; Second Court, Sadar, Chittagong for a claim of Taka 24,91,063.01 against M/S. Janapad Enterprise and its sole proprietor Iftekharul Alam (proforma respondent Nos. 2-3). His case, in brief, is that the defendants purchased the M.V. Silver Port for Cutting and scrapping and for that purpose they entered into several agreements with the plaintiff. The defendant also agreed to pay Taka one lac for storing the materials after the cutting and breaking of the vessel on the land belonging to the plaintiff at Mouza Bhatiari for a period of one year from 1st April, 1982. The plaintiff completed the work of cutting by 30th September, 1983. As the defendant did not pay his bills he filed the suit for realisation of his dues. After filing the suit the appellant prayed and obtained an order of attachment before judgment against the scheduled articles. The appellant's suit was decreed on 29th March, 1984. Money Execution Case No. 56 of 1984 was instituted for the execution of that decree. Meantime, respondent No. 1, the Pubali Bank Limited, filed an application on 8th January, 1984 under Order 38 rule 8 read with Order 21, rules 58 and 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure for investigation and release of the attached property, and Miscellaneous judicial case No. 1 of 1984 was registered. 

 29. The respondent Bank's case is that in the usual course of its business the Bank granted credit facilities to respondent Nos. 2 and 3 as per terms and conditions contained in the letter of sanction dated 11th January, 1982 for the import of the M.V. Silver Port for the purpose of scrapping and that the vessel was pledged to the Bank as a security for the loan. It was agreed that the entire dismantling work of the imported Vessel be made under the direct supervision of the Bank's branch at Agrabad ; that on arrival of the ship at Chittagong sufficient number of godown-keepers and godown chowkiders should be posted round the clock at the breaking site of the ship at the importer's own shipyard at Bhatiari, Chittagong ; and that an Officer of the Bank would supervise the work of godown-keepers, godown chowkiders and the people engaged for breaking the ship. Respondents 2 and 3 also undertook to deposit all sale proceeds to the Bank's Stadium Branch through its Agrabad Branch, Chittagong ; to provide warehouse facilities which could be controlled by the Bank personnel and security guards; and to deposit, on demand by the Bank, all local expenditures including custom duty, income tax, breaking cost, incidental costs, bank charges and interest. It was also agreed that the importer would repay the L/C value along with bank charges entirely within stipulated period of 120 days from the date of handing over the vessel to the Bank, and, in the event of failure to retire the bills by paying the Bank's dues on demand, the Bank would dispose of the ship to adjust the liabilities. As per repayment arrangement respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were to break the vessel at their cost and then take delivery of the scraps from the Bank for selling those in the market, and before the actual delivery of the scraps the sale proceeds were to be deposited with the Bank. Accordingly, on the application of respondent Nos. 2 and 3 the delivery orders were issued to them. Further case of respondent No. 1 is that in spite of repeated demands respondents Nos. 2 and 3 neglected in repayment of the loan which stood at Taka 16,09,853.07 on 23rd November, 1983. In order to realise the outstanding loan the Bank decided to dispose of the pledged scrapped materials through auction and published a tender notice in daily news papers on 11.11.1983 and 12.11.1983. While the Bank was taking steps to sell the pledged ship-scraps, the appellant filed Money Suit No.137 of 1983 on 22.11.1983 to frustrate the said auction sale, and obtained an order of attachment by deliberately sup-pressing the fact that the ship-scraps were pledged with the Bank and the scraps were in the lawful custody of the Bank. 

 30A. After examination of the relevant documents, namely, photo copy of the pledge of goods, the authorisation letter given by respondents 2 and 3 to their Manager, M.A. Quasem, for taking delivery of the goods on payment ; the delivery orders of the Bank in favour of M/s. Janapad Enterprise and the tender notice and the delivery certificate of the vessel, the High Court Division held that the vessel M. V. Silver Port was imported for scrapping purpose on the loan, sanctioned by the Bank, and that the vessel was pledged with the Bank. The High Court Division set aside the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the vessel was pledged, but not the scraps. From exhibits 5 and 7 series the High Court Division held that the scraps of the vessels were taken out from time to time by the authorised agents of the defendants from the possession of Bank. The High Court Division also set aside the finding of the lower court that the Bank did not take any step to realise its dues. In fact the Bank published advertisement for auction of the pledged goods, but the auction was stopped due to the proceeding between the parties and the parties knew about the matter. By the impugned order dated 5th July, 1987 the High Court Division vacated the trial Court's order of attachment, released the scheduled articles from attachment and directed that Money Execution Case No. 56 of 1984 be struck off. 

 31. On behalf of tile appellant it is submitted that the High Court Division failed to distinguish between the right of a pledgee and that of a mortgagee and that even if the goods were treated as pledged goods the Bank could, as a pledgee, get release of the attached goods under Order 21 rule 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that the Bank as a pledgee could not have more right than the owners themselves and that the owners could exercise their right over the attached goods only after paying the service charge of the petitioner. It is. submitted that the appellant is entitled under Section 170 of the Contract Act to retain the attached goods as bailee till he receives due remuneration for the services rendered for cutting, breaking and scrapping of the vessel. It is also submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in striking off Money Execution Case No. 56 of 1984 in a miscellaneous proceeding like the instant one. 

 32. With regard to the appellant's first contention the respondent Bank submits that the question of distinction between mortgage and pledge is agitated for the first time in this Court. It is also submitted that it had never been a case of the appellant that he was a bailee of the ship-scraps. The appellant's case has althrough been that no pledge of the scraps has been created in favour of the Bank, but after considering the documents and oral evidence adduced in the case the High Court Division held that the scraps of the ship were duly pledged with the Bank. 

 33. Let me first consider the decision reported in 28 DLR (AD) 43 which appears at the first glance to support the appellant's case. In that case the judgment debtor obtained an order of attachment directing the Government to deposit the judgment-debtor's security-money lying with the Government. The Government moved the High Court Division in revision against the order of attachment. The High Court Division upheld the order of attachment. On appeal this Court held that the order of attachment would subsist subject to the prior lien or charge of the Government. The money lying in court was ordered to be transferred to the custody of the Government to satisfy its prior lien or charge. It was observed that though the judgment debtor had no dominion over the security money he had the full right of ownership and power of disposal in respect of the sum of money that might be left after discharging his liabilities to the Government and that the judgment creditor would have the same right as the judgment-debtor had over that money. The learned Counsel for the appellant after taking a cue from these observations submitted that in this case also the appellant has entered into the shoes of the judgment-debtor and he has the same right of ownership and power of disposal with regard to the ship scraps subject to the charges that may be payable to the Bank. This is an attractive argument. The facts of the instant case are, however, clearly distinguishable from those of the cited one. In the reported case the security money was the judgment debtor's own money. Here the vessel was purchased by the money advanced by the Bank for the sole purpose of scrapping to be under-taken by the judgment-debtor under the control and supervision of the Bank. The judgment-debtor has no right of ownership or power of disposal as an ordinary owner. If one is to go all the way with the reported decision then the possession of the attached goods is to be returned to the Bank. But in this case the possession is already with the Bank. In the reported decision the security money was a certain sum. In this case the claim of the Bank and that of the plaintiff are to be ascertained before any meaningful adjustments of claims and counter-claims of the parties could be settled. The Court cannot take upon itself such a task in an interlocutory proceeding of attachment. The party seeking attachment of properties in possession of a third party must make out a clear case. 

 34. Eighteen different items of goods valued at Taka 8,78,000.00 were sought to be attached by the plaintiff-appellant. Out of them one item is with regard to scraps, 88 tons, valued at Taka 8,8,000/- There is no evidence to show that all the remaining items like plates, ladders, shafts, propellers, angles, pipes, boiler etc. were used for cutting or scrapping to give rise to the appellant's claim of lien over them for the works done by him. In this case the plaintiff could have exercised his right under section 170 of the. Contract Act if he had possession over the scheduled materials. The High Court Division's finding on the basis of the documents on record and the evidence adduced in the matter that the Bank had although been in possession of the attached goods does not suffer from any infirmity. In that view of the matter the plaintiff will be precluded from relying on the decisions, cited above, in support of his alleged claim to retain the scheduled properties as a bailee. In fact, the plaintiff did not make out any case that he was entitled under section 170 of the Contract Act to retain the scraps as a bailee till he received due remuneration for the services rendered by him. In the application for attachment the plaintiff did not mention the word 'lien' nor did he do so in his written objection to the application for vacating that order. The plaintiff did not disclose that the vessel was pledged to the Bank. He did not make any complaint to the Bank that he was not paid his dues by the defendants. Before the learned Subordinate Judge the Bank produced a series of documents and also examined one witness. The plaintiff however, did not produce any paper nor did he examine any witness in support of his case. The learned Subordinate Judge did not at all consider the Bank's documents exhibit-6 series by which the defendants asked for delivery orders from the Bank, and exhibits-7 series by which the Bank gave the delivery orders on deposit of money. The plaintiff's application for attachment itself indicates that he was not in possession of the scheduled goods. Had he been in possession, he would have asked for an order of injunction and not for attachment. 

 36. It has been submitted that the High Court Division ought to have in all fairness and in equity upheld the order of attachment, as in this case the plaintiff will be left without any remedy if the Bank is allowed to sell the scheduled good by auction. In this case equity is not in favour of the plaintiff. From the facts and circumstances of the case I have got no hesitation to hold that the plaintiff knew about the defendant's transaction with the Bank and that the vessel with all its materials was pledged to the Bank. The contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the Bank ought to have proceeded against the defendant's other securities has got no substance. Under the provisions of section 176 of the Contract Act, 1872 as well as under the terms of the transactions the defendants entered into with the Bank, the latter is free to follow any of the ways legally available to it for realisation of its dues. The Court will refrain from making any officious direction that the Bank should follow a particular security or collateral and give a sportive chance to the plaintiff to realise his dues. 

 37. The appellant's last contention is that the High Court Division erred in law in striking off the money execution case. The actual words of the High Court Division's order in this regard are Let the money execution case No. 56 of 1984 relating to the attached property be struck off. I am of opinion that the High Court Division did not strike off the execution case itself. In any case, to avoid any further confusion, I make it clear that the order of the High Court Division vacating the trial court's order of attachments only upheld. The money execution case will follow its own course. With this observation the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
